perendiē — the day after tomorrow (Traupman 86; Plaut. Merc. 2.3.41 crās agitō, perendiē agitō; Cic. Att. 12.44.3); crās — tomorrow.
hōrās īnspicere — check the time (Traupman 89); hōrologium īnspicere — look at the clock or watch (Traupman 122).
tempus fallere — pass the time (Traupman 89).
crepusculum, crepusculī n. — twilight, dusk (Traupman 89; Plaut. Cas. prol. 40); crepusculō — at dusk.
autoraedā īnscēnsā temperī profectī sunt — they got into the car and set off in good time (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
Diū exspectātum est, patre subinde hōrās in tēlephōnō īnspiciente — There was a long wait, Dad checking the time on his phone every so often (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).

«Haec quoque,» inquit avia, «perendiē cum patre tuō vidēbis, sed vēra et magna.» — “You’ll see these too,” said Grandma, “the day after tomorrow with your dad, but real and big.” (Fābula III, Apud avum et aviam).
dōnec avia, hōrologiō īnspectō, «Domum,» inquit. «Prandium parandum est.» — until Grandma looked at her watch and said, “Home. Lunch has to be made.” (Fābula III, Apud avum et aviam).
Ad aditum dēnique, ut tempus fallerent, per lūsum latitāvērunt et quaeritāvērunt — Finally, at the gate, to pass the time, they played hide and seek (Fābula VI, Reditus: per Alpēs domum).
Trāmine commūnī per crepusculum Lisbōnam rediērunt — They went back to Lisbon on the slow train at dusk (Fābula II, Sintra: castellum et puteus).

english: Exclamations: oh no! / hey! / wow! / hooray! / here, take it! / truly
keywords: exclamations interjections oh no hey hey you wow hooray hurrah here take it truly vocabulary 29 October fabulae Theodōrus et pater

items.html: Atat! — oh no!, of a sudden realisation (Plaut.; Ter.).
Heus! — hey!, to get attention; Heus tū! — hey, you! (Plaut.; Ter.; Cic.).
Papae! — wow! (Plaut.; Ter.).
Iō! — hooray!, in two syllables (Hor. C. 4.2.49 iō triumphe); Euax! — hooray!, as in the airport entry.
Em! — here!, handing something over; Accipe, em. — here, take it; Em manum! — here’s my hand (see the safety entry).
nae — truly, indeed, with a pronoun: Nae tū bene meministī. — You remember well, you do.
Atat, lapis deest! Lapis mēcum dormit! — Oh no, the stone’s missing! The stone sleeps with me! (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
Ibi pater, «Heus, dā mihi manum!» identidem clāmitāns — There Dad, calling out again and again, “Hey, give me your hand!” (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
«Heus tū!» inquit pater, custōdem agēns. «Quis es?» — “Hey, you!” said Dad, playing the guard. “Who are you?” (Fābula V, Lisbōna: castellum et ōceanārium).
«Papae,» inquit puer, «etiam autoraedā longā vehimur!» — “Wow,” said the boy, “we’re going on a bus too!” (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
«Iō, septem! Septem vehiculīs vectus sum!» — “Hooray, seven! I’ve been on seven vehicles!” (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
«Accipe, em. Ita tenē: laeva ministeriō, dextra est intenta labōrī.» — “Here, take it. Hold it like this: the left hand helps, the right does the work.” (Fābula IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
Nae tū bene meministī — You remember well, you do (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).

english: Coming! / wait a moment / hurry / do you get it? / I get it / you’re right / really? / what now?
latin: Jam aderō. · Manē dum! · Jam teneō!
keywords: coming I’ll be right there wait a moment wait a minute hurry up quick at once do you understand get it I understand I see you’re right really what now is that enough in suspense can’t wait itching vocabulary 29 October fabulae Theodōrus et pater

items.html: Jam aderō. — I’ll be right there, coming! (Traupman 101).
Manē dum! — wait a moment! (Traupman 90, 110).
Mātūrā! Mātūrāte! — hurry up! (Traupman 101); āctūtum — at once (Plaut.; Ter.).
Jam tenēs? — do you get it now?; Jam teneō! — now I get it! (Traupman 99).
Bene dīxistī. — you’re right, well said (Traupman 107).
Ain' vērō? — do you really mean it?; the answer is Ajō. (Traupman 103; Plaut.; Ter.).
Quid nunc? — what now? (Traupman 104); Satin' est? — is that enough?, will this do? (Traupman 97).
animī pendēre — be in suspense (Traupman 108); gestiō, gestīre + infinitive — be itching to (Traupman 101; Cic.).
«Jam aderō,» inquit pater. — “Coming,” said Dad. (Fābula II, Sintra: castellum et puteus).
«Mātūrā,» inquit pater. «Raeda mox aderit.» «Jam aderō, tata!» — “Hurry up,” said Dad. “The taxi will be here soon.” “Coming, Dad!” (Fābula VI, Reditus: per Alpēs domum).
Pater «Manē dum!» clāmābat — Dad kept calling, “Wait a moment!” (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).

«Agedum,» inquit pater, «onerā palliolō umerōs tuōs, et āctūtum sequere mē.» — “Come on,” said Dad, “put your little coat on your shoulders and follow me at once.” (Fābula II, Sintra: castellum et puteus).

Mendum est sīcut lapillus in calceō tuō: nōn bene ambulās, dōnec lapillum invēneris et ējēceris. Jam tenēs? — A bug is like a pebble in your shoe: you can’t walk properly until you find the pebble and throw it out. Do you get it now? (Fābula III, Apud avum et aviam).
«Tū obrigado, quia puer es.» «Jam teneō!» — “You say obrigado, because you’re a boy.” “Now I get it!” (Fābula IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
«Nōn attulit! Mīnōtaurus Conimbrigae manet!» «Bene dīxistī.» — “He didn’t bring it! The Minotaur stays at Conimbriga!” “You’re right.” (Fābula III, Apud avum et aviam).
«Theodōrus fēcit,» inquit pater. «Ain' vērō?» inquit avus. — “Theo made it,” said Dad. “Did he really?” said Grandpa. (Fābula IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
«Quid nunc faciēmus, tata?» — “What shall we do now, Dad?” (Fābula IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
«Satin' est, tata?» «Satis est; rēctē factum.» — “Is that enough, Dad?” “That’s enough; well done.” (Fābula IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
Theodōrus, animī pendēns, «Ut tē jūvit crustum, ave?» inquit. — Theo, in suspense, said, “How did you like the pie, Grandpa?” (Fābula IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
«Gestiō gustāre!» «Post cēnam gustābimus.» — “I’m itching to taste it!” “We’ll taste it after dinner.” (Fābula IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).

english: We’re fine / so far so good / I’m having fun / take care / let me catch my breath / let me go / stop right there / that’s enough / why so sad?
keywords: how are you we’re fine so far so good having fun take care look after yourself catch my breath let me go let go stop stop right there that’s enough take it easy why so sad what’s the matter thank you please vocabulary 29 October fabulae Theodōrus et pater

items.html: Bene habēmus. — we’re fine (Traupman 105); Bellē adhūc. — so far so good (Traupman 108); Mihi bene est. — I’m having a lovely time (Traupman 109).
Cūrā ut valeās. — take care of yourself, the close of Cicero’s letters (Traupman 94).
Sine respīrem, quaesō. — let me catch my breath, please (Traupman 95); to several, Sinite respīrem.
Mitte mē! — let me go!; Mitte mē, sīs! — let go of me, please! (Traupman 99, 102; Plaut.).
Stā īlicō! — stop right there! (Traupman 108; īlicō “on the spot”, Ter.).
Parce! — that’s enough!, take it easy! (Traupman 102, 108).
Quid tū es tam trīstis? — why so sad? (Traupman 99); Quid tibi est? — what’s the matter? (Traupman 92).
Amō tē. — thank you, for a kindness done (Traupman 109; Plaut.); amābō — please, with an imperative (Plaut.; Ter.).
«Rēctēne advēnistis?» inquit avia. «Bene habēmus,» inquit pater. — “Did you have a good journey?” said Grandma. “We’re fine,” said Dad. (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
Mediō itinere «Bellē adhūc,» inquit. — Halfway along he said, “So far so good.” (Fābula II, Sintra: castellum et puteus).
«Mihi bene est, tata!» inquit puer. — “I’m having a lovely time, Dad!” said the boy. (Fābula V, Lisbōna: castellum et ōceanārium).
«Cūrā ut valeās, mī fīlī,» inquit avia. — “Take care of yourself, my son,” said Grandma. (Fābula VI, Reditus: per Alpēs domum).

«Sinite respīrem, quaesō,» inquit. «Vōs mūrōs ascendite; ego hīc vōs exspectābō.» — “Let me catch my breath, please,” he said. “You go up on the walls; I’ll wait for you here.” (Fābula V, Lisbōna: castellum et ōceanārium).

In scālīs mōbilibus cum Theodōrus, «Mitte mē, tata!» clāmitāns, manū patris dīmissā sōlus stāre vellet — When Theo, on the escalator, kept shouting “Let me go, Dad!” and wanted to let go of his hand and stand by himself (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).

Theodōrō ad orbitās properante, «Stā īlicō!» inquit pater. «Dā mihi manum.» — As Theo hurried towards the tracks, Dad said, “Stop right there! Give me your hand.” (Fābula V, Lisbōna: castellum et ōceanārium).
nunc per lectum in latus sē volūtat, quoad pater «Parce!» inquit — now rolls sideways across the bed, until Dad says, “That’s enough!” (Fābula VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae).

«Quid tū es tam trīstis, pāvō?» inquit. «Nōlī trīstis esse! Etiam sine caudā pulcher es!» — “Why are you so sad, peacock?” he said. “Don’t be sad! You’re handsome even without a tail!” (Fābula V, Lisbōna: castellum et ōceanārium).
«Quid tibi est? Aurēs dolent?» — “What’s the matter? Do your ears hurt?” (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
«Bene factum,» inquit avia. «Amō tē.» — “Well done,” said Grandma. “Thank you.” (Fābula III, Apud avum et aviam).
«Id, amābō,» inquit, «adjuvā mē, tata!» — “Help me with it, please, Dad!” he said (Fābula IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
Bonō animō es! — Cheer up! (Cic. Att. 5.18); see the Feelings II entry for more.

english: Quiet and gestures: in a low voice / finger to the lips / point / on tiptoe / slip away / creep out
keywords: quiet quietly in a low voice whisper shh finger to lips point pointing tiptoe slip away sneak out creep crawl out vocabulary 29 October fabulae Theodōrus et pater

items.html: summissā vōce; vōce summissā — in a low voice.
digitō silentium suādēre — put a finger to the lips for silence (cf. Ov. Met. 9.692 digitōque silentia suādet).
digitum ad aliquem intendere — point at someone (Traupman 98); digitō intentō — pointing.
suspēnsō pede — on tiptoe; sē subdūcere — slip away quietly.
prōrēpō, prōrēpere, prōrēpsī — creep out, crawl out (Hor. S. 1.1.37).

Pater digitō silentium suāsit. Theodōrus, quī alibī clāmāre solet, hīc vōce summissā «Pluteī sunt, tata,» inquit, «sīcut avī, sed aurātī.» — Dad put a finger to his lips. Theo, who shouts everywhere else, said here in a low voice, “They’re bookshelves, Dad, like Grandpa’s, but golden.” (Fābula III, Apud avum et aviam).

Theodōrus pittam cum cucurbitulīs, melongēnīs, piperītidibus rubrīs poposcit, nōn per patrem sed ipse, digitō in imāginem intentō. — Theo asked for the pitta with courgettes, aubergines and red peppers, not through Dad but himself, pointing at the picture. (Fābula VI, Reditus: per Alpēs domum).
Tum, cum puer artē dormīret, suspēnsō pede sē subdūxit — Then, when the boy was fast asleep, he slipped away on tiptoe (Fābula VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae).
lōdīce rejectā prōrēpsit et ad fenestram accessit — threw off the blanket, crawled out and went to the window (Fābula II, Sintra: castellum et puteus).

items.html: scandō, scandere — climb or clamber. L&S gives no perfect or supine for this verb; none is invented here. See also playground movement verbs.
ascendō, ascendere, ascendī, ascēnsum — go or climb up.
dēscendō, dēscendere, dēscendī, dēscēnsum — go or climb down.
dēsiliō, dēsilīre, dēsiluī — jump down; the infinitive has long ī.
perveniō, pervenīre, pervēnī, perventum — reach, arrive at.
Vīsne scandere? — Do you want to climb?
Scandāmus. — Let’s climb.
Scande, Theodōre. — Climb, Theo.
Dēscende lentē. — Climb down slowly.
Nōlī dēsilīre. — Don’t jump down.
Ad summum pervēnistī. — You’ve reached the top.

items.html: prehendō, prehendere, prehendī, prehēnsum — grasp, take hold of.
teneō, tenēre, tenuī, tentum — hold, keep holding; contrasts with taking hold in the first place.
dīmittō, dīmittere, dīmīsī, dīmissum — let go of, release.
tangō, tangere, tetigī, tāctum — touch; useful for reaching far enough to touch a hold.
attollō, attollere — lift or raise. L&S gives no perfect or supine.
trahō, trahere, trāxī, tractum — pull, draw.
nītor, nītī, nīsus sum / nīxus sum — lean or bear upon, support oneself, push upward; deponent. The supporting limb or object may be in the ablative.
Ansam firmiter tenē. — Hold the hold firmly.
Potesne illam ansam tangere? — Can you touch that hold?
Pedem dextrum attolle. — Lift your right foot.
Tē sūrsum trahe. — Pull yourself upward.
Pedibus nītere. — Push with your feet / support yourself on your feet.
Hanc ansam dīmitte. — Let go of this hold: use only when releasing that particular hold is intended.

english: Splash / sprinkle / drench / slap the water / don’t splash / that’s enough
keywords: splash splashing sprinkle soak drench water fight pool bath too much enough

items.html: spargō, spargere, sparsī, sparsum — scatter, splash water (on someone); perfundō, perfundere, perfūdī, perfūsum — drench, pour all over. Diana splashing Actaeon: sīc hausit aquās vultumque virīlem perfūdit, spargēnsque comās ultrīcibus undīs — “she scooped up water, drenched the man’s face, and splashing his hair with the avenging water…” (Ov. Met. 3.189–190).
aspergō, aspergere, aspersī, aspersum — sprinkle, spatter; frequent in ritual, but everyday too: adspersistī aquam, “you’ve splashed water on me” (Plaut. Truc., quoted by L&S).

plangō, plangere, plānxī, plānctum — strike with a smack; aquam palmīs plangit — he slaps the water with his palms, modelled on plangēbant aliae prōcērīs tympana palmīs (Catull. 64.261). plangor, plangōris m. — the slap of water, of waves (Catull. 64.273). Avoid plānctus, which nearly always means beating the breast in mourning.
Nōlī aquam spargere! — Don’t splash!
Nōlī aquam plangere! — Don’t slap the water!
Nimis spargis! — You’re splashing too much!
Modo tantum aquae spargēbās! — You were splashing so much earlier!
Hoc nimium est! Satis est! — That’s too much! That’s enough!
Ōhē, jam satis est! — Whoa, that’s enough now! (Hor. Serm. 1.5.12–13; Mart. 4.89.1)

english: Feelings II: sorry / ashamed / bored / fed up / cross / grumpy / cheer up / don’t worry / calm down / surprised / shy
latin: mē paenitet · mē pudet · taedet · stomachor, stomachārī
keywords: sorry apologise regret ashamed embarrassed bored boring fed up sick of it cross grumpy crabby moody touchy irritable bad temper tantrum angry lose temper cheer up don’t worry don’t be upset calm down control yourself glad for you cheerful gloomy scared surprised amazed shy bashful homesick good mood

items.html: mē paenitet (+ gen. or infinitive) — I’m sorry, I regret it (Traupman 157, 383). An apology for a child: Sī quid perperam fēcī, mē paenitet. — If I’ve done anything wrong, I’m sorry (Traupman 112).
mē pudet (+ gen.) — I’m ashamed (Traupman 93); Ecquid pudet? — Aren’t you ashamed? (Cordier).
taedet; pertaedet — I’m bored, fed up (Traupman 96, 107): taedet jam audīre eadem mīliēns — “I’m sick of hearing the same thing a thousand times” (Ter. Ph. 487). Taedetne tē? — Are you bored?

mōrōsus, mōrōsa, mōrōsum — grumpy, peevish (Traupman 151; Cic. Sen. 65). stomachor, stomachārī — be cross, in a huff (Cic.); stomachōsus, stomachōsa, stomachōsum — touchy, irritable (Traupman 158; Hor.). īrācundus, īrācunda, īrācundum — hot-tempered (Traupman 154); īrācundiā efferrī — lose one’s temper; īrācundiam cohibēre — keep one’s temper (Traupman 392).
suscēnseō, suscēnsēre + dat. — be cross with: nihil fēcit quod suscēnseās — he did nothing for you to be cross about (Traupman 93; Ter., Cic.).
Bonō animō es! — Cheer up! (Cic. Att. 5.18; Plaut. Merc. 3.1.33, in L&S); Traupman’s Habē animum bonum! (150). hilarus / hilaris — cheerful; maestus — gloomy (Traupman 150, 153).
Nōlī sollicitārī! — Don’t worry! (Traupman 409); Nōlī perturbārī. — Don’t be upset (Traupman 110).
Tē continē. — Control yourself (Traupman 96); Compēsce mentem! — Keep your cool! (Traupman 101); aequō animō — calmly.
Gaudeō tuā causā. — I’m glad for you (Traupman 18).

items.html: improbus, improba, improbum — naughty; petulāns, petulantis — cheeky (Traupman 350); nēquam (indecl.) — good-for-nothing, rascal (Traupman 99) (vōx cōmica: Plaut., Ter.).
lascīvus, lascīva, lascīvum — playful, frisky, up to tricks (Traupman 110); of young animals in Horace and Vergil.
frūgī (indecl.) — good, well-behaved: Frūgī homō es — “you’re a good lad” (Ter. Ad. 959); sum bonus et frūgī (Hor. Ep. 1.16.49). Traupman 99: frūgī es.

oboediēns, oboedientis + dat. — obedient (Traupman 352); the classical idiom is dictō audiēns — doing as one is told (Cato Agr. 142; Cic. Phil. 7.2).
ineptus, inepta, ineptum — silly; Nōlī ineptīre! — Don’t be silly (Traupman 107; Ter. Ad. 934; Catull. 8.1 dēsinās ineptīre).

obstinātus, obstināta, obstinātum; pertināx, pertinācis — stubborn (Traupman 158; L&S).

animulus, animulī m. — darling, only in the vocative: mī animule (Traupman 151; Plaut. Cas. 1.46, in L&S; Cordier). dēliciae, dēliciārum f. — darling: Tulliola, dēliciae nostrae (Cic. Att. 1.5.8). Plautus’s string meus ocellus, meum labellum … meum mel, meum cor (Poen. 366–367).
Improbe! Quid fēcistī? — You rascal! What have you done?
Frūgī es: omnia tua reposuistī. — Good boy: you’ve put all your things away.
Venī hūc, mī animule. — Come here, my darling.

english: Give it here! / really? / why so? / what happened? / ouch! / nonsense! / never mind / excuse me / of course / no way
latin: Cedo! (pl. cette) · Itane? · Quid ita? · Oiei!
keywords: give it here hand it over give me pass me tell me really is that so why how come what happened ouch ow oh dear nonsense rubbish never mind let it go leave me alone stop it cut it out don’t interrupt stop bickering look me in the eye excuse me sorry with pleasure of course why not no way that’s right I think so it doesn’t matter I can’t take it any more I’m done for it’s no use good luck who is it it’s me quiet

items.html: Cedo! (plural cette) — give it here! hand it over! tell me! An old imperative from -ce + the root of dō, with short e and short final o (L&S cĕdo; de Vaan s.v. cedo); it takes an object: Cedo manum. — give me your hand (Plaut. Capt. 859, Most. 332). Not cēdō, cēdere “go, give way”. Terence: Nōlō, volō; volō, nōlō rūrsum; cedo, cape (Ph. 950); Plautus: Vigilō, cedo bibam (Most. 373b) (Traupman 99, 104).
Itane? — Really? Is that so? (Traupman 101; Plaut., Ter.); see also Ain’ vērō? in the Coming! entry.
Quid ita? Quīdum? — Why so? How so? (Traupman 101) (vōx cōmica: Plaut., Ter.). Quidnī? / Quippinī? — Why not? Of course (Traupman 111; Ter. And. 315).
Quid factum est? — What happened? (Traupman 100).
Oiei! — Ouch! Oh dear! (Traupman 105; Ter. Eun. 4.4.47, Ph. 4.3.58, in L&S). Vae miserō mihi! — Oh dear me! (Traupman 104).
Nūgās! / Nūgae! — Nonsense! (Traupman 104); Aufer nūgās (Plaut. Truc. 861); Nūgās agis (Plaut. Men. 621).
Sine! — Never mind! Let it be (Traupman 104). Omitte mē! — Leave me alone! (Traupman 102). Dēsine! / Dēsiste! — Stop it! (Traupman 96).
Nōlī mihi obloquī! — Don’t interrupt me! (Traupman 101); Nōlī interpellāre (Traupman 33). Dēsinite rīxārī. — Stop bickering (Traupman 36).
Aspicedum contrā mē. — Look me in the eye (Traupman 97; Plaut.).
Ignōsce mihi. — Excuse me, sorry (Traupman 97); Mē tibi excūsō. — I apologise (Traupman 93). libenter — with pleasure (Traupman 105).
Amō tē. / Multum tē amō. — Thank you (so much) for what you’ve done (Traupman 109), the idiom of Cicero’s letters.

scīlicet, profectō — of course (Traupman 105); Minimē! / Nūllō modō! — No way! (Traupman 104); Sīc est. / Ita est. — That’s right (Traupman 107, 109); Sīc opīnor. / Ego nōn putō. — I think so / I don’t think so (Traupman 109).
Nīl interest. — It makes no difference (Traupman 96); Patī nequeō amplius. — I can’t take any more (Traupman 109).
Periī! / Interiī! — I’m done for! (Traupman 96) (vōx cōmica); Īlicet. — It’s no use (Traupman 110) (vōx cōmica: Plaut., Ter.).
Fēlīciter! — Good luck! (Traupman 103); Quis homō est? — Ego sum. — Who is it? — It’s me (Traupman 111); Fac silentium! — Quiet! (Traupman 367; Plaut. Pers. 4.3.50).
Cedo istum lapidem! — Give me that stone!
Cette manūs, ambō; viam trānsīmus. — Give me your hands, both of you; we’re crossing the road.

blocks.html: cĕdo (short e, short final o) is a different word from cēdō, cēdere (“go, give way”); L&S lists them separately. The lexicon writes it without macrons: Cedo, cette.

items.html: marītus, marītī m. — husband (Traupman 24); caelebs, caelibis — single (Traupman 20). in mātrimōnium dūcere — marry (of the man) (Traupman 21); nūbō, nūbere, nūpsī + dat. — marry (of the woman).
parentēs, parentum m. — parents; līberī, līberōrum m. — children (Traupman 24). Cicero: nātūrā fierī ut līberī ā parentibus amentur (Fin. 3.62).
patruus, patruī m. — uncle, father’s brother; avunculus, avunculī m. — uncle, mother’s brother (Traupman 24).
amita, amitae f. — aunt, father’s sister; mātertera, māterterae f. — aunt, mother’s sister (Traupman 24).
fīlius frātris / sorōris; fīlia frātris / sorōris — nephew; niece (Traupman 24; Traupman 351).
nepōs, nepōtis m.; neptis, neptis f. — grandson; granddaughter (Traupman 24); pronepōs, pronepōtis m. — great-grandson (Comenius 119); proavus, proavī m. — great-grandfather (Traupman 24).

socer, socerī m. — father-in-law; gener, generī m. — son-in-law; nurus, nurūs f. — daughter-in-law (Traupman 24; Erasmus: Socer uxōris meae pater est mihi. Gener fīliae meae marītus … Nurus fīliī meī uxor). affīnis, affīnis m./f. — an in-law (Traupman 24).
lēvir, lēvirī m. — husband’s brother; glōs, glōris f. — husband’s sister (Traupman 24; both rare, Dig.). Traupman’s plainer phrases: marītus sorōris, uxor frātris (283, 379).
vitricus, vitricī m.; noverca, novercae f.; prīvignus, prīvignī m.; prīvigna, prīvignae f. — stepfather, stepmother, stepson, stepdaughter (Traupman 24; Cic.).
cognātus, cognātī m.; cognāta, cognātae f. — relative (Traupman 24).

stirps, stirpis f. — family tree, lineage (Traupman 24, 313 adds stemma); majōrēs, majōrum m. — ancestors. Traupman 24 gives atavī for forefathers, but strictly atavus is a great-great-great-grandfather (L&S).
frāterculus, frāterculī m.; sorōrcula, sorōrculae f. — little brother; little sister (Traupman 24; Juv. 4.98; Plaut. fr.); fīliola, fīliolae f. — little daughter (Traupman 24).
major / minor / maximus / minimus nātū — older, younger, eldest, youngest (Traupman 21, 23): Quis frāter est maximus nātū?
Jack’s rule: familia is the household, not “wife and children” (use suī, domus); Traupman 24 lists it as “family”.
Hic est patruus tuus, frāter patris. — This is your uncle, Dad’s brother.
Uter est major nātū, tū an cōnsōbrīnus tuus? — Who’s older, you or your cousin?

items.html: īnfāns, īnfantis m./f. — baby (Traupman 24); recēns nātus — newborn (M-O, 17th century). Neo-Latin Lexicon s.v. baby: īnfantulus (Apul., post-classical), neonātus (Helfer), recēns nātus, modo nātus.

pūsiō, pūsiōnis m. — little boy (Cic. Tusc. 1.57); Traupman 410 gives puerculus, which is late (Arnobius). frustum puerī — “you scrap of a boy!” (Traupman 336; Plaut. Pers. 5.2.68, in L&S) (vōx cōmica).

chīramaxium, chīramaxiī n. — pram, baby carriage (Traupman 275; M-O chīramaxium īnfantile, warning against the spelling chīromaxium); in Petronius a small hand-drawn carriage. Neo-Latin Lexicon adds vehiculum puerīle (Bauer, Helfer). See the trolley entry for chīramaxium sarcinārum.
laguncula īnfantilis — baby bottle (M-O); M-O’s titina is late medical Latin. subligāculum īnfantile — nappy (M-O, modern; classically subligāculum is a loin-cloth).
gerula, gerulae f. — nanny, child-carrier (M-O; Tert., post-classical); nūtrīx, nūtrīcis f.; nūtrīcula, nūtrīculae f. — nurse, nanny (Cic.; Hor. Ep. 1.4.8 quid voveat dulcī nūtrīcula majus alumnō).
lallō, lallāre — sing a lullaby; lallum, lallī n. — lullaby (M-O; Pers. 3.18 īrātus mammae lallāre recūsās; Aus.).
geminī, geminōrum m.; gemellī, gemellōrum m. — twins (L&S; Erasmus et quidem gemellōs); trigeminī — triplets (M-O; Liv. 1.24).

fasciae, fasciārum f.; incūnābula, incūnābulōrum n. — swaddling clothes (Plaut. Truc. 5.13, in L&S: fasciīs opus est, pulvīnīs, cūnīs, incūnābulīs). Comenius: Īnfāns involvitur fasciīs, repōnitur in cūnās (Orbis pictus 120).
dentītiō, dentītiōnis f. — teething (M-O; Plin.); dēns īnfantilis / dēciduus — baby tooth (M-O); dēns mōbilis — loose tooth (M-O; Plin.).
paedotrophēum, paedotrophēī n. — kindergarten (Traupman 336, modern coinage); conclāve īnfantium — nursery (Traupman 352).

nāscor, nāscī, nātus sum — be born (Traupman 282); obstetrīx, obstetrīcis f. — midwife (Plaut., Ter.); gravida; praegnāns — pregnant (L&S, classical; not in either source); parturīre — be in labour (M-O).
cum magnus eris; cum adolēveris — when you’re big, when you’ve grown up. Traupman 324 gives juvenēscō, but that means “reach youth, grow young again” (Hor., Ov.), not a child’s growing up.
Cum magnus eris, ipse birotā vehēris. — When you’re big, you’ll ride a bike yourself.
Tū quoque in cūnīs vāgiēbās, cum īnfāns erās. — You too used to cry in your cradle when you were a baby.

latin: diēs nātālis · nātālīcia, nātālīciae f. · nātālīcium, nātālīciī n.

items.html: diēs nātālis; nātālis, nātālis m. — birthday (Traupman 280; M-O s.v. birthday; Cic., Hor.). Cicero’s little girl met him nātālī suō ipsō diē — “on her very birthday” (Att. 4.1.4).
Fēlīcem nātālem (tibi exoptō)! — Happy birthday! (Traupman 280).

nātālīcia, nātālīciae f. — birthday party: dat nātālīciam in hortīs — “he’s giving a birthday party in his gardens” (Cic. Phil. 2.15, as cited in L&S); nātālīciam dare / agitāre — throw a birthday party (Traupman 280).
nātālīcium, nātālīciī n. — birthday present (Traupman 280; Censorinus, in L&S).

lībum nātālīcium — birthday cake (Traupman 280); lībum, a cheese cake, was the Roman birthday offering. Cato’s recipe: lībum hōc modō facitō (Agr. 75). Ovid’s birthday shared with his brother: ūna celebrāta est per duo lība diēs — “one day was celebrated with two birthday cakes” (Tr. 4.10.12).
Horace’s birthday questions: nātālīs grātē numerās? — “do you count your birthdays gladly?” (Ep. 2.2.210).
Crās est diēs nātālis tuus! Quot annōs nātus eris? — Tomorrow’s your birthday! How old will you be?
Hoc tibi nātālīcium est. — This is your birthday present.

items.html: Quota hōra est? — What time is it? (Traupman 81, 89; M-O s.v. time: what time is it?; Hor. S. 2.6.44 hōra quota est?). Also Quot hōrae sunt? (Traupman 89). hōrās quaerere — ask the time (M-O, citing Plin. 7.182).
Quotā hōrā …? — At what time …? (Traupman 81). Est prīma ferē hōra. — It’s about one o’clock (Traupman 81).

sēmihōra, sēmihōrae f. — half an hour (Traupman 87, 330; M-O s.v. hour: 30 minutes; Cic.); also dīmidium hōrae (Traupman 87). sesquihōra, sesquihōrae f. — an hour and a half (Traupman 87, printed sēsqui-; Plin. Ep. 4.9.9). Lewis & Short leaves the e unmarked, so it is unmarked here.

ūncia / sextāns / triēns / bēs hōrae — five / ten / twenty / forty minutes (M-O s.v. hour), the classical twelfths applied to the hour. For the quarter and three quarters (quadrāns, dōdrāns) see the telling-the-time entry.

hōrologium parietārium — wall clock (Traupman 403); hōrologium manuāle / bracchiāle — wristwatch (M-O s.v. watch, which prints brachiāle); index, indicis m.; digitus, digitī m. — clock hand (M-O s.v. hand, from Vives).

hōrologium arēnārium; clepsammidium, clepsammidiī n. — hourglass, sand timer (M-O s.v. hourglass); classical clepsydra is a water-clock. chronoscōpium (Traupman 386) / chronometrum (M-O s.v. stop-watch) — stopwatch.
Quota hōra est, tata? — Septima ferē. — What time is it, Dad? — About seven.
Sēmihōram exspectā; deinde lūdēmus. — Wait half an hour; then we’ll play.
Spectā: ubi est index parvus? — Look: where’s the little hand?

items.html: merīdiēs, merīdiēī m. — noon; merīdiē — at noon (Traupman 88). media nox — midnight; mediā nocte — at midnight; dē mediā nocte — around midnight (Traupman 86–87).

items.html: kindergarten: Traupman gives paedotrophēum (336), not in Lewis & Short. day-care, nursery: Traupman gives nēpiagōgium (301), Morgan–Owens paedodochīum and brephodochīum (M-O s.v. day-care center). All are modern Greek formations, and none is settled.
in lūdum īre — go to school (M-O s.v. school types: elementary school, citing Plaut.); Traupman gives scholam frequentāre and scholam obīre (31).

magister, magistrī m.; magistra, magistrae f. — teacher (Traupman 32, 391); litterātor, litterātōris m.; litterātrīx, litterātrīcis f. — primary teacher (Traupman 32; L&S: “a teacher of reading and writing”); lūdī magister — schoolmaster (M-O s.v. teacher; Cic.).
classis, classis f. — class (Traupman 28); conclāve scholāre — classroom (Traupman 28); lēctiō, lēctiōnis f. — lesson (Traupman 339); Morgan–Owens gives schola for one class meeting (M-O s.v. class).
homework: Traupman gives pēnsum domesticum (29, 329), Morgan–Owens pēnsum domī faciendum (M-O s.v. assignment: homework). Classically a pēnsum is the day’s allotment of spinning.
pausa, pausae f. — break, recess (Traupman 31; L&S: ante- and post-classical).
tabula ātra / alba — blackboard / whiteboard (Traupman 28, 32); the Vatican lexicon gives tabula litterāria.

latin: Cōnsīde. · Attende. · Eho, nōn tam cito!
keywords: classroom commands instructions sit down sit up straight listen pay attention look at me put your hand up raise your hand speak up louder lower your voice quiet stop talking stop squabbling stop arguing not so fast whoa never mind a word with you may I go to the toilet bathroom

items.html: Cōnsīde (cōnsīdite). — Sit down. Rēctē sedē. — Sit up straight (Traupman 34).
Audī dīligenter. Attende (attendite). — Listen carefully. Pay attention (Traupman 33–34). Converte oculōs in mē. — Look at me (Traupman 33).
Attolle manum. — Put your hand up (Traupman 34).
Ēloquere. — Speak up. Remitte vōcem. — Lower your voice (Traupman 33–34).
Dēsine loquī. — Stop talking. Dēsine rīxārī. — Stop squabbling (Traupman 34; rīxor is classical).
Eho, nōn tam cito! — Whoa, not so fast! (Traupman 34); eho is the interjection of comedy (Plaut.; Ter.).
Sine. — Never mind (Traupman 33). Paucīs tē volō. — I want a word with you (Traupman 33; Ter. Andr. 29).
Licetne mihi in lātrīnam īre? — Licet. — May I go to the toilet? — Yes (Traupman 28, 32).
Cōnsīde, quaesō, et attende: fābulam narrābō. — Sit down, please, and listen: I’m going to tell a story.
Vōs ambō, dēsinite rīxārī! — You two, stop squabbling!

blocks.html: Left out: Traupman 33’s nōlī eum taxāre for “don’t tease him”. In Lewis & Short taxō means “touch sharply; censure” (post-Augustan), not “tease”.
